cards.prompt: Gut check: is a billion seconds longer or shorter than 30 years? Make your guess before revealing.
cards.reveal: Longer. A billion seconds is about 31.7 years. The useful intuition: a million seconds is about 11.6 days, but a billion seconds is more than three decades.

cards.prompt: Two people enter a room. What are the odds they share a birthday: closer to 1 in 365, 1 in 180, or 1 in 30?
cards.inputHint: Pick one and explain your instinct...
cards.reveal: For two people it is about 1 in 365. But with only 23 people, the chance that some pair shares a birthday is already above 50%. Pairwise comparisons grow surprisingly fast.

cards.prompt: You buy a $20 cinema ticket, then lose it outside. Would you pay another $20 to see the film? What bias might influence you?
cards.inputHint: What would you do, and why?
cards.reveal: The sunk cost effect can make the lost $20 feel relevant even though the decision now is simply whether the film is worth another $20 to you.

cards.prompt: Why can you see lightning before you hear thunder? Explain it without using the word ‘faster’.
cards.inputHint: Explain it in your own words...
cards.reveal: Light covers the distance from the storm to you almost instantly at everyday scales. Sound has to propagate through air and takes roughly 3 seconds per kilometre.

cards.prompt: ‘Zeitgeist’ literally combines the German words for what two things?
cards.reveal: Zeit means time and Geist means spirit or mind. Hence ‘spirit of the age’.

cards.prompt: A headline says a food ‘doubles your risk’ of a disease. What number do you need before deciding whether that is scary?
cards.reveal: The baseline risk. Doubling a risk from 1 in 1,000,000 to 2 in 1,000,000 is very different from increasing it from 1 in 4 to 1 in 2.

cards.prompt: Someone gives you evidence against a belief you strongly hold. What is one question you can ask yourself to detect whether you are moving the goalposts?
cards.inputHint: Write the question you would ask yourself...
cards.reveal: Try: ‘Would I have accepted this standard of evidence if it supported my position?’ It is a practical test for motivated reasoning.

cards.prompt: You have three tasks: 5 minutes and important, 60 minutes and important, 20 minutes and unimportant. Which do you start first, and why?
Name a decision you are postponing. What new information would genuinely change your choice?
Turn a boring household object into a $100 product. Pick the object and give it one feature people might actually pay for.
Explain Wi-Fi to an intelligent 8-year-old in two sentences. No jargon allowed.
Sell someone an umbrella without mentioning rain, water or weather.
Memorise these four words for a later card: cactus, violin, moon, suitcase. Build one ridiculous mental image linking all four.
Without scrolling back, can you recall the four objects from the memory challenge?
cards.reveal: The four were cactus, violin, moon and suitcase. A vivid linked image usually beats repetition because it gives memory more retrieval cues.

cards.prompt: You earn 5% interest each year. Roughly how long does money take to double: 7, 14 or 28 years?
cards.reveal: About 14 years. The Rule of 72 gives a quick estimate: 72 divided by the interest rate gives approximate doubling time.

cards.prompt: In a negotiation, why can asking ‘How am I supposed to do that?’ be more useful than saying ‘No’?
cards.reveal: It rejects the current proposal without ending the conversation and shifts some problem-solving back to the other person.

cards.prompt: Your phone distracts you 20 times a day. Which is stronger: relying on willpower or changing one part of the environment? Give one environmental change.
A café queue is too slow, but you cannot hire staff or make coffee faster. Give three ways to reduce the customer’s perceived wait.
In programming, what is a variable? Explain it using something from a kitchen.
cards.reveal: A variable is a named place for a value that can be read or changed. A labelled container is a useful analogy: the label stays while the contents can change.

cards.prompt: A chart starts its vertical axis at 95 instead of 0. Why might two small differences suddenly look enormous?
cards.reveal: Truncating the axis magnifies the visible distance between values. It can be legitimate, but it can also exaggerate the apparent size of a difference.

cards.prompt: Pick one thing you want to improve. What is the smallest version you could practise for five minutes today?
A concert ticket you own could sell for $200. You would never pay $200 to attend. What does keeping the ticket really cost you?
cards.reveal: The opportunity cost is roughly the $200 you give up by attending instead of selling. Ownership can obscure the real trade-off.

cards.prompt: Make this sentence vivid: ‘The man was tired.’ You may add only eight words.
Which teaches you more: rereading a page three times or closing it and trying to reconstruct the main ideas? Why?
cards.reveal: Active recall usually produces stronger learning than passive rereading because retrieving information strengthens access to it and exposes gaps.
